blocks.content: Kubernetes networking is built on one foundational requirement: every Pod gets its own real, routable IP address, and every Pod can reach every other Pod directly, cluster-wide, with no network address translation involved at all.
1. Every Pod Gets Its Own Real IP
blocks.text: 1. Every Pod Gets Its Own Real IP

blocks.content: Unlike the Docker containers covered throughout the Docker course, which typically share a host's IP behind NAT, every single Kubernetes Pod gets its own genuinely routable IP address within the cluster's network.

blocks.alt: A real, individually routable IP, for every single Pod

blocks.content: Any Pod can open a connection directly to any other Pod's IP, with no network address translation happening along the way, this is a deliberate, foundational design decision, not an incidental detail.

blocks.alt: A direct connection, exactly as if both were on the same simple network

blocks.content: 3. A Real Departure From Docker's Default Model
blocks.text: 3. A Real Departure From Docker's Default Model

blocks.content: This is worth contrasting directly with what the Docker Networking module covered, Docker's default bridge network uses NAT for outbound traffic, and containers are not directly reachable from outside without explicit port publishing. Kubernetes's Pod network deliberately works differently, a genuinely flat network where every Pod is already reachable.

blocks.alt: NAT and port publishing by default, versus an already-flat, directly reachable network

blocks.content: 4. A Requirement, Not Just a Convenience
blocks.text: 4. A Requirement, Not Just a Convenience

blocks.content: This flat, NAT-free model is not optional or incidental, it is a formal requirement every Kubernetes networking implementation, provided by a CNI plugin covered later in this module, must actually satisfy for the cluster to function correctly.

blocks.alt: A formal requirement, not a nice-to-have, that networking plugins must genuinely deliver

blocks.content: 5. Working Across Nodes, Not Just Within One
blocks.text: 5. Working Across Nodes, Not Just Within One

blocks.content: Critically, this direct reachability is not limited to Pods on the same physical node, a Pod on node A can reach a Pod on node B just as directly as it could reach one on its own node, the cluster network genuinely spans every node as one address space.

blocks.alt: Direct reachability spanning the entire cluster, not just a single node

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Every Pod gets its own routable IP, and any Pod can reach any other Pod directly, with no NAT involved, a foundational, formally required design decision.
This is a genuine departure from Docker's default NAT-based networking, and it works identically whether the two Pods share a node or are on entirely different ones.
